x.text:
Tag writes >50% of my PRs every day. It also does ~100% of my data analysis, and fixes most of our product feedback + bugs.

It's not like a regular Slack bot. It is proactive, programmable, it has memory, it has access to your connectors. With Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, it has strong judgement.

Example prompts I use:

- "@Claude react to threads in this channel with ✅ when resolved"
- "@Claude from now on, attempt to repro every bug in this channel end to end, running the full app. once you reproduce the bug, put up a pr to fix it and tag the right team for code review"
- "@Claude brainstorm ~100 hypotheses for what could explain this weird data, use a workflow to in/validate. spend 10m tokens or so digging very deep. draw a chart with the result."
- "@Claude make me an interactive game explaining how this part of the code works, then make a slide deck explaining it for others on the team"

https://t.co/gmsALM8Lvs

x.text:
We're helping world-class organizations like @klaviyo build agentic deployment platforms.

① Connect every agent (claude, codex, cursor…)
② Configure SSO via their IDP (Okta, Entra)
③ Now everyone can cook, securely®

What happens to SaaS once every company sets this up? I get this question a lot 😁

First, the data must come from somewhere. These apps only work if they can be infused with business data.

This is why we see the big enterprise SaaS players suddenly prioritize shipping CLIs and MCPs. Or dust off APIs they were neglecting for years.

The new 'procurement bar' will be how ergonomic your product is for *agents*, rather than humans. How easily they can navigate your ontology and work with your data.

Once that's in place, there's a long tail of SaaS applications that I suspect will never be bought again. They'll be generated. They'll be more secure, more performant, more modern, and tailored to each company's and employee's needs.
x.bio: @vercel CEO
x.textZh:
我们正协助 @klaviyo 等世界级机构构建智能体部署平台。

① 连接所有智能体（Claude、Codex、Cursor……）
② 通过其身份提供商（IdP）配置单点登录（Okta、Entra）
③ 现在，人人皆可烹饪，且安全无忧®

一旦每家公司都搭建起这套体系，SaaS 行业将发生什么？我经常收到这个问题 😁

首先，数据必须来自某个地方。只有当应用能够融入业务数据时，它们才能发挥作用。

这就是为什么我们看到大型 SaaS 企业突然优先开发 CLI 和 MCP，或者重新启用那些被搁置多年的 API。

新的“采购门槛”将取决于你的产品对 *智能体* 的易用性，而非对人类。智能体能否轻松导航你的本体论结构并与你的数据交互，将成为关键。

一旦这一基础就位，我怀疑将有一长串 SaaS 应用不再被购买。它们将被生成出来。它们会更安全、更高效、更现代化，并针对每家公司和每位员工的需求量身定制。

x.text:
You can’t automate what you can’t measure. This means that evals are one of the gates to diffusion of AI in the enterprise. 

We can test our deterministic processes through software, but most enterprises have no useful way of understanding how their non-deterministic processes are working today. Specifically the work that agents are doing for them.

Evals are mission critical for enterprises adopting AI because you have no other way of knowing what’s working, what’s broken, what changed, what improved, what you can do more of, etc. if you don’t have a good sense of how agents work in your environment today. All changes, upgrades, and deployments are downstream from good evals.

Not only are we going to get vastly more domain specific evals over time for the labs and across the industry, but every enterprise will also need a clear sense of how agents are performing in their environment as well. Huge opportunity.
x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
x.textZh:
你无法自动化你无法衡量的事物。这意味着评估（evals）是 AI 在企业中普及的关键关卡之一。

我们可以通过软件来测试确定性流程，但大多数企业目前缺乏有效的方法来理解其非确定性流程的运作情况，特别是智能体（agents）为他们所做的工作。

评估对于采用 AI 的企业至关重要，因为如果你不清楚智能体在当前环境中的工作方式，你就没有其他途径知道哪些有效、哪些失效、哪些发生了变化、哪些得到了改进，或者哪些可以加大投入。所有的变更、升级和部署都依赖于良好的评估结果。

随着时间推移，我们不仅会在实验室和行业层面获得大量领域特定的评估方法，每个企业也需要明确了解智能体在其环境中的表现。这是一个巨大的机遇。

The biggest design mistake I made when we moved OC to sqlite: using sync db access. When it was just an agent that reports to you on Slack or iMessage this was fine; now that one agent might do 50 sessions in parallel and the whole team works on it, it is limiting.

I have a /goal with Astra that so far landed 575 PRs to move everything to to async workers. We ship these improvements as we make progress. Pretty insane how even huge refactors are no longer scary.

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Sequence Holdings Co-Founder and CEO Michael Lee
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:25
Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required. You think about your typical investment in a fund, and you're typically trying to figure out how do we start to package to sell this thing in three That is just a very different framing for how we think about technological transformation and what what are the investments you're willing to bring to bear here. What we do is scarce. We're trying to do one deal per year.

Speaker 1 | 00:25 - 00:26
That's it. Our job is to do one.

Speaker 2 | 00:33 - 00:58
Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, I'm here with Michael Lee, cofounder and CEO of Sequence Holdings. They just announced the largest AI take private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000. We talk about this, the Sequence story, how AI transformation is actually going to permeate the economy and what transfers from public investing to private equity to operating.

Speaker 2 | 00:58 - 01:01
Welcome, Michael. Michael, thanks for doing this.

Speaker 1 | 01:01 - 01:02
Thanks for having me.

Speaker 2 | 01:02 - 01:18
So you started Sequence Holdings, which is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound their businesses to be market leaders with AI. We should talk about that, and it's a very exciting model. But you also announced this big transaction in Baldwin. Tell us about it.

Speaker 1 | 01:18 - 01:53
Yeah. You know, we started the company twenty months ago really with an eye towards can we partner with world class businesses and management teams, working closely with our frontier engineering team to forge market leaders. The brokerage space is an area that we've been spending a lot of time on since the founding of the business. We've met dozens of insurance brokers, and Baldwin was truly N of one of all the insurance brokers that we've met. It was it's been a privilege over the last few months to spend a lot of time with Trevor Baldwin and the management team, and we could not be more excited about the journey that lies ahead between us, the Baldwin team, and the Dell family office that supported us in this transaction.

Speaker 2 | 01:54 - 02:09
I want to zoom all the way out to a little bit about, you know, your background, you and your co founder Alex, how this idea for Sequence came about, because you've been, you know, an investor, now, you know, a hybrid investor operator. Like, tell me about how you arrived at the idea to begin with.

Speaker 1 | 02:09 - 02:15
You know, when I first joined Lone Pine in 2017, one of the first areas that I was asked to cover was AI.

Speaker 2 | 02:16 - 02:17
That's actually quite early.

Speaker 1 | 02:17 - 02:38
Yeah. It was, you know, as I'm sure you recall, it's kind of when AlphaGo came out. It's actually when the first transformer paper came out, and there was a lot of excitement at the time around what would be commercially viable if you scale these architectures. And at the time, these were convolutional neural nets, GANs, LSTMs, and the like. And, you know, I think we all know how the story ends, which is we obviously saw a lot of exciting things come out of it.

Speaker 1 | 02:38 - 03:15
But as you scaled these architectures, there were degrading effects over time to scale. You know, I share that context because, you know, when the models came out or ChatGPT came out at the end of twenty two, you know, what became obvious to me at least is that the world had forever changed. You know, we finally had an architecture that we knew could scale infinitely. Now, whether or not that was possible, what would come from that was not clear, but we knew we did know that we could scale with compute, that the architecture would improve. And, you know, like an investor, I started to think about what were the impacts to the world, and I kind of felt strongly that AI would have an uneven impact on the economy.

Speaker 1 | 03:15 - 03:27
There are certain parts of the economy that I felt that AI just wouldn't impact at all. Right? Take restaurants, golf courses, things like that. There are certain industries that I just felt like a startup would win. Right?

Speaker 1 | 03:27 - 04:07
Take coding, for example. Like, Conviction and Sequence going to go buy an outsourced coding services business feels like a terrible idea, which you will give money to Cognition or toanthropic. But there, as a student of business, there have always been certain industries where I felt like the incumbent had all the advantages, and that could be brand, that could be scale, network effects, regulatory. And in light of what is going to be the biggest technological shift of lifetime, I felt very strongly that if you could acquire the right incumbent, inherit the advantages of being that incumbent, could you forge the market leader? And the kernel of that idea is the one that really is upon which Sequence was founded upon.

Speaker 1 | 04:07 - 04:36
Came up with the idea in early twenty three, had a handful of people try to get me to leave Lone Pine to go do it then. Just wasn't the right time for me. And then I remember going for a walk with my wife in '24, letting her know that, hey, it's pretty rare in life to be in the middle of the most important technological change of our lifetime. Having the kernel of an idea, I felt very strongly about, and feeling very strongly that I could pull together the team to go and pull it off. And so that's why we started a sequence and couldn't be more excited about kind of what we've been able to achieve to date and kind of what we see ahead of us.

Speaker 2 | 04:36 - 05:01
It's a super first principles approach to, you know, what is the macro chain to this happening technology? How's it going to impact the economy? But, you know, many investors, at least venture investors, would be like, oh no, incumbents have a bunch of advantages. I guess it's just not for us. How did you think about, you know, scale and the idea of being able to engage with or even own incumbents?

Speaker 2 | 05:01 - 05:05
That's a, I guess you can just do things, but that's an ambitious premise.

Speaker 1 | 05:06 - 05:37
I think it's more just, it's the business model that meets the opportunity today. So like if we take a giant step back, you know, and at least at sequence, when we think about what's happening with AI today, we think we're living through the equivalence of the next industrial revolution. And, you know, what we generally see in most enterprises, what I typically see from a lot the software companies that are producing AI agents today, is this giant push to give small machines to every human in the human assembly line and to speed up work. And like, there's nothing wrong with that. That's great.

Speaker 1 | 05:37 - 06:22
It's better than nothing. But as you know, when you have machines that can work 20 fourseven, that can scale with electricity, that can accomplish what no individual human or group of humans can do, the right answer is to think about how do you start to reorganize what an organization should be to meet the opportunity of what's available to you with technology. And that's the context upon which we're sitting in. And I think for the, really in the first time, we have a real opportunity here to partner with amazing companies, with great leadership teams, partnering with our platform and our engineering team, and really thinking critically around how do we reorganize the organization? How do we lean into what's best in terms of what the technology can do, what can humans do, and rethink how we can compete in these various industries?

Speaker 1 | 06:23 - 06:32
And I think it's just really more of an opportunity piece more so than an ambition piece in that, like, I just think this has to happen, and I don't see it a natural way for it to happen unless you do it through our approach.

Speaker 2 | 06:32 - 06:43

本期播客邀请Sequence Holdings联合创始人兼CEO Michael Lee，探讨在AI时代如何通过“永久控股公司”模式对传统行业巨头进行AI重塑。Lee分享了公司近期与戴尔家族办公室合作、以77亿美元收购保险经纪公司Baldwin的案例，并阐述了核心投资与运营逻辑：
1. 瞄准有护城河的 incumbent：AI对经济的影响是不均衡的，在品牌、规模、监管和网络效应占优的传统行业，收购并重塑现有巨头比扶持初创企业更具确定性。
2. 独特的控股公司架构：采用永久控股公司模式，将资本期限与长期深度运营承诺对齐。公司文化以“工程师”为核心，通过自建平台Atlas实现技术规模化复用，并高度重视组织变革与员工体验的“人类工程”。
3. 已验证的运营成效：以BankSouth银行为例，AI系统使消费贷款审批时间缩短94%，整体放款周期从30天降至11天，在不增加人手的情况下实现贷款量翻倍，让员工聚焦高价值工作。
4. 长期主义投资哲学：区别于传统PE的基金周期，Sequence坚持“每年只做一笔交易”的稀缺策略，坚信在庞大市场中押注“卓越的执行团队”是穿越技术周期的核心。
